items.title: Bela Fleck interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, December 7, 2004
items.q: I play some Bach, and I know what that is, and I’ve never written anything on a level of that complexity or depth.

ctx.x: Well I think they were asking about that a lot of the material you write and perform is pretty complex from chord structures and melodies, and then when you guys start improvising it can get very complex. Yet you still felt that there was a simplicity about it that people who might not understand it technically can still like –

Right. All right. Well it just depends what you’re comparing it to. Because I mean if you’re listening to great classical music or if you’re listening to different kinds of jazz through different periods or Indian music, our music would be just pretty simple. You know what I mean? So it depends on the context of what you’re comparing it to. I mean if you’re used to listening to jam bands, or just straight ahead bebop just in four-four that’s complex in the soloing, but the rest of it, the structures can be, I…

feels like it’s in four. If we’re looking for an eleven, we want it to feel like it’s in four. We want to find a way to make what seem to be more complex forms feel very natural and comfortable. But that’s something people have been doing for a long time too. So I’m very aware of the overall context of music, the centuries of music or as much of it as I’ve been exposed to and what’s actually new about our group is probably just a combination of things that haven’t come together before. But in terms of reinventing…
